scenes.title: Start with a recent experience
scenes.visual: Adult visitor approaches a fictional venue entrance.
scenes.narration: Your snapshot describes a group. Now explore one experience from beginning to end. A customer journey is the sequence of steps a person takes toward a goal. Start with a recent account or a clearly labeled planned observation, not the features of your future app.

scenes.title: Define the goal and boundaries
scenes.visual: Editable start, goal and finish cards.
scenes.narration: What is the person trying to achieve? Finding registration before a session is a goal; opening an app is usually a means. Define where this experience begins and ends. Keep motivation and success criteria unknown if you have not asked.

scenes.title: Map what happens today
scenes.visual: Visitor follows signs, asks staff and reaches check-in.
scenes.narration: Record the current steps and contact points: signs, a website, a staff member or a desk. Note what helps as well as what may create difficulty. A helpful staff interaction may resolve the problem. Do not invent waiting times, frequency or complaints to justify a product.

scenes.title: Separate action from emotion
scenes.visual: Editable action, reported feeling and unknown cards.
scenes.narration: An action can be observed. A feeling usually needs the person’s own account. Someone looking around is not proof of frustration. Label reported feelings, interpretations and unknowns separately. Never manufacture a quote or assign emotions based on appearance.

scenes.title: Choose a learning question
scenes.visual: Observer reviews a neutral question on a notebook.
scenes.narration: Look for the step with the most useful uncertainty. Ask about a recent experience: what happened, what they tried and what mattered. Keep the question neutral. A difficulty is not proof that people will switch or pay, and one account does not represent everyone.

scenes.title: Build your learning map
scenes.narration: Create your Customer Journey and Learning Map: group and source, goal and boundaries, before, during and after steps, helpful and difficult moments, evidence limits and a next question. Keep the map revisable. Next you will learn how to research without guessing.

sections.label: 02 / LEARN
sections.heading: Understand the experience before designing a solution.

children: A
goal
is what the person wants to achieve. A
journey
is the sequence of steps they take. A
contact point
is where they interact with information, people or a service. A
frustration
is a difficulty or feeling that needs evidence; do not assume it from an observed action.
Illustrative example:

a first-time visitor wants to reach registration before a session. They look at directions, ask staff and arrive at a desk. Staff help may work well. Looking around does not establish confusion, frustration or delay.
Map the current experience
Choose one group and one specific experience from Lesson 11.
Define the start, finish and intended outcome.
Record before, during and after steps, with the source of each account.
Include useful moments and difficulties; avoid a pain-only story.
Separate actions, reported feelings, interpretations and unknowns.
Choose one neutral question that could change the map.
Use “planned — not yet observed” when you lack a real account. Leave times, frequency and intensity unknown unless sourced. A single experience is a clue, not a representative customer journey.
Review customer snapshot
Review alternatives log

blocks.prompt: You see a visitor looking around near registration.

options.label: They are definitely frustrated
options.feedback: Keep the observation separate from interpretation. Do not infer frustration or payment from looking around.

options.label: They looked around; their reason and feeling are unknown
options.feedback: Useful distinction: looking around is an action; reason and feeling remain unknown until investigated.

options.label: They will pay for my app
options.feedback: Keep the observation separate from interpretation. Do not infer frustration or payment from looking around.

Simulated Coach · no AI connection
Try four scripted guidance modes. The preview reads your current worksheet locally; it does not send information anywhere.

replies.teach: Map a current experience around a goal. Separate actions from reported feelings; include what helps and keep unknowns visible.
replies.guide: Set boundaries, record before/during/after steps, source each claim and choose a neutral question. Avoid mapping your future app instead of current behaviour.
replies.review: Journey Map check: {missing} required fields still empty. This scripted check counts fields only; it cannot verify steps, feelings, sources or demand.
replies.challenge: Did you infer frustration? What works already? What would change the map? Are quotes, timing and frequency actually sourced?

sections.label: 05 / CHALLENGE
sections.heading: Challenge the story in your map.

children: More questions to discuss
What already works? Are you mapping a product you want to build rather than current behaviour? Are times and frequency sourced? Can people decline? Have you treated one journey as universal?
Answer all three. You can retry; all three correct are required for local completion.
